title: Polynomial-time EFX for three additive agents
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(C,k\ge 1\) such that, for every finite set of goods and every three nonnegative rational additive valuations, A returns a complete EFX allocation in at most \(C(N+1)^{k}\) steps, where N is the binary input length and EFX has the all-goods convention below?
why: The smallest unresolved computational case for exact EFX after existence for three agents was established.

progress.text: Complete EFX existence for three additive agents is proved constructively, with a pseudopolynomial algorithm.
Polynomial-time EF2X for three agents is obtained, while the paper explicitly retains the exact EFX computational gap.
A preprint reports polynomial-time approximate EFX for up to eight agents, a different guarantee from exact EFX.

definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and \(m\ge 0\) goods indexed by \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\). The input gives m and each value \(v_{i},g=p_{i},g/q_{i},g\) with integers \(p_{i},g\ge 0\) and \(q_{i},g>0\) encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle \(S\subseteq [m], v_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}v_{i},g\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_{1},A_{2},A_{3})\) of \([m]\); bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in \(\{1,2,3\}\). It is EFX if \(v_{i}(A_{i})\ge v_{i}(A_{j}\setminus \{g\})\) for every \(i,j\in \{1,2,3\}\) and every \(g\in A_{j}\), including goods with \(v_{i},g=0\). The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty \(A_{j}\) gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.

context_blocks.title: Every possible removed good matters
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

context_blocks.title: Existence has already been proved
context_blocks.text: Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

context_blocks.title: Why pseudopolynomial time is insufficient
context_blocks.text: A value as large as \(2^{\mathrm{L}}\) needs only \(\mathrm{L}+1\) binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

context_blocks.title: Nearby guarantees do not give exact EFX
context_blocks.text: Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.

sentences: Three agents must receive all indivisible goods under nonnegative additive valuations.
An allocation is EFX when removing any one good from another agent’s bundle would eliminate the first agent’s envy.
Such allocations are known to exist for three agents, including when values are zero or tied.
The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the binary valuation table’s length.
Pseudopolynomial constructions and polynomial algorithms for weaker fairness guarantees do not settle this target.
